Paper_name: Good Me Bad Me: Prioritization of the Good-Self During Perceptual Decision-Making
Summary: The study investigates which aspects of the self-concept drive the prioritization of self-related stimuli. Using a shape-label association task, participants learned to link shapes to 'good-self', 'bad-self', 'good-other', and 'bad-other' concepts. Results showed that responses were consistently faster and more accurate for shapes associated with the 'good-self' compared to all other shapes, regardless of whether the task focused on self-relevance or valence. A hierarchical drift diffusion model analysis revealed that this 'good-self prioritization effect' was driven by a faster rate of evidence accumulation (information uptake) for good-self stimuli. This demonstrates that the positive, identity-centered aspect of the self is crucial for facilitating perceptual decision-making.
Author: Chuan-Peng Hu, Yuxuan Lan, C. Neil Macrae, Jie Sui
Conclusion: The main finding is that perceptual decision-making is exclusively facilitated by activation of the 'good-self' representation. The self-prioritization effect is not a general bias for all self-related information but is specifically driven by the positive, identity-based aspect of the self-concept ('good me'). Computational modeling indicated this effect stems from a more efficient rate of information processing for good-self stimuli, not from changes in response caution or non-decision time. This clarifies that the core, morally good self is the crucial component producing self-bias in perceptual tasks.
